description: We are a team of five, combining technology, research and innovation. Vikrant and Swarup led the technical development of AeroMed, handling its architecture, core functionality and software implementation. Palash, Aleesha and Kruti led the research, exploring astronaut health challenges, studying physiological parameters and shaping the project's scientific foundation. Together, we transformed our ideas into a platform aimed at making astronaut health monitoring smarter and more personalized.
summary:
AeroMed: Project Summary
Team Parallax Tensor | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

On long missions, the body changes gradually, and messages to Earth take minutes, so crews increasingly have to spot health problems themselves. Fixed health limits make this harder. A resting heart rate that is normal for one astronaut can be a warning sign for another.

AeroMed is early-warning software that runs on board. It tracks five daily wearable signals: resting heart rate, HRV, sleep duration, sleep timing and skin temperature. Over the first 14 days it learns each astronaut’s personal baseline, then freezes it so a slow decline cannot become the new normal.

From day 15, fixed rules sort changes into three levels. Watch means one signal has shifted. Act means two or more signals have changed together for days. Escalate means Act has lasted two days, or the crew member has pressed the red-flag button. No AI makes these decisions, so every alert can be explained.

In a simulated 45-day mission, AeroMed caught a planted illness on days 22 to 24 and raised no alerts for healthy crew. Results come from synthetic data, and the thresholds still need clinical validation.
details:
AeroMed — Because Space Exploration Shouldn't Come at the Cost of Astronaut Health 🚀

1. What Does AeroMed Do and How Does It Work?

Imagine being millions of kilometres away from Earth, working inside a confined spacecraft, with no immediate access to a hospital. What if your body starts showing subtle signs of stress, but nothing seems obviously wrong yet?

That's the problem we wanted to address with AeroMed.

AeroMed is an onboard astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to identify subtle physiological changes before they develop into potential mission risks.

Unlike conventional monitoring systems that compare everyone against generic health limits, AeroMed learns what is normal for each astronaut individually and looks for changes from that personal baseline.

Here's how it works:

Step 1: Getting to Know the Astronaut

AeroMed collects five primary daily health signals from wearable devices:

  • Resting Heart Rate (RHR)
  • Heart Rate Variability (HRV – RMSSD)
  • Sleep Duration
  • Sleep Timing
  • Peripheral Skin Temperature

Activity data is also incorporated for additional context.

During the first 14 days, the system observes these readings and builds an individual health baseline using robust statistical methods such as Median and scaled Median Absolute Deviation (MAD).

Think of it as getting to know an astronaut's normal routine before trying to identify anything unusual.

Once established, this baseline is frozen so that gradual deterioration doesn't quietly become the new normal.

Step 2: Spotting What Doesn't Look Normal

From Day 15 onwards, AeroMed compares new readings against the astronaut's personal baseline using a deterministic, rule-based detection engine.

It doesn't simply look at isolated numbers. It searches for patterns across multiple physiological signals and consecutive days.

The system has three alert levels:

  • WATCH: A meaningful deviation is detected in an individual signal. Time to pay closer attention.
  • ACT: Multiple signals show aligned changes that persist over several days, indicating a pattern that warrants attention.
  • ESCALATE: The ACT condition persists for two consecutive days, or the astronaut manually raises an urgent symptom flag for medical review.

A two-day hysteresis mechanism helps prevent unnecessary fluctuations between alert levels.

Every alert explains exactly what has changed, how it differs from the astronaut's normal baseline and what the recommended next steps are.

No mysterious AI predictions. No unexplained warning codes. Just transparent rules and understandable health information.

Step 3: Seeing Health, Not Just Numbers

We wanted AeroMed to be more than another dashboard filled with graphs and statistics.

That's why we built an interactive 3D Astronaut Digital Twin. It allows users to explore different body systems and see where physiological deviations are relevant. Selecting a category opens more detailed information, trends and baseline comparisons.

The platform also includes:

  • 45-Day Mission Replay: Travel through the mission timeline, revisit historical physiological changes and understand how an astronaut's health evolves.
  • Earth Reference Cohorts: Compare individual trends against non-diagnostic reference populations for additional context.
  • Intelligent Notes Assistant: Interact with an intelligent assistance layer that interprets verified telemetry, summarizes health trends and helps medical officers understand complex information through natural-language explanations.

The intelligent assistance layer works alongside the core statistical engine. It supports interpretation and accessibility, while all physiological alerts remain controlled by deterministic rules.

Step 4: Staying Functional Even When Earth Is Far Away

Space missions cannot depend on having a perfect internet connection.

AeroMed is designed to work onboard during communication delays and blackouts. Health check-ins, medical reviews and other records can be stored locally and synchronized when communication becomes available.

The crew can continue monitoring their health even when Earth isn't immediately reachable.

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

We believe astronauts shouldn't have to wait until something becomes visibly wrong before paying attention to their health.

AeroMed aims to make that possible through:

  • Personalized Monitoring: Identifies changes that generic health thresholds might miss because every astronaut has a different physiological normal.
  • Earlier Awareness: Helps detect gradual patterns such as autonomic stress, circadian disruption, sleep debt and possible shared illness-like trends.
  • Fewer Unnecessary Alerts: Requires multiple signals to align and persist before raising higher-level alerts. In our simulated evaluation, ACT and ESCALATE alerts occurred on approximately 2% and 0.5% of days, respectively.
  • Explainable Decisions: Every alert is backed by measurable changes and predefined rules. AI does not decide whether an astronaut receives an alert.
  • Onboard Autonomy: Continues providing monitoring and decision support even during communication blackouts.
  • Better Accessibility: Converts complex physiological information into understandable insights through interactive visualizations and the intelligent Notes Assistant.

Our Bigger Vision

We started by thinking about astronauts, but the underlying problem isn't limited to space.

People working in isolated environments, such as polar research stations, ships and remote healthcare facilities, face similar challenges. We believe personalized, offline-capable health monitoring could eventually make a difference there too.

3. Tools, Technologies and Resources Used

We combined web technologies, statistical analysis, intelligent assistance and 3D visualization to bring AeroMed to life.

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5 and CSS3.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express for APIs, data handling and real-time updates through Server-Sent Events (SSE).
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js for the interactive astronaut digital twin, anatomical telemetry mapping and mission visualization.
  • UI and Charts: Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons and custom charts for physiological trends and baseline comparisons.
  • Statistical Intelligence: Robust baseline calculations using Median, scaled MAD, logarithmic HRV transformation and circular sleep-timing calculations.
  • Intelligent Decision Support: An intelligent assistance layer for contextual telemetry analysis, health-trend summarization and natural-language interaction, supported by a deterministic offline processing engine.
  • Data Resources: Public PhysioNet heart-rate and sleep datasets from four volunteers, used to inform the creation of a synthetic 45-day astronaut crew dataset.
  • Wearable Compatibility: Modular integration architecture designed for existing consumer wearables through authorized HTTPS webhooks, Web Bluetooth heart-rate support and compatible Apple HealthKit, Garmin Health API and Oura Cloud payloads.
  • Testing: Automated Node.js tests to verify baseline calculations, alert rules, data validation, simulation isolation and mission replay.
  • Presentation: Canva.

One important design decision: we didn't build custom wearable hardware. Instead, AeroMed is designed around physiological signals that compatible consumer wearables already collect.

4. What Makes AeroMed Different?

It learns the person before judging the numbers.

Most basic monitoring systems ask: "Is this reading too high or too low?"

AeroMed asks: "Is this unusual for this particular astronaut?"

That small change in perspective is the foundation of our project. By learning an individual's baseline and then freezing it, AeroMed aims to identify gradual changes that could otherwise go unnoticed.

But we didn't stop at monitoring.

1. An Anatomical 3D Digital Twin

Instead of presenting disconnected numbers, AeroMed maps physiological information onto an interactive astronaut model, making complex health information easier to explore and understand.

2. Mission Replay and Scenario Simulation

The 45-day mission timeline allows users to revisit different stages of a mission and observe how health indicators evolve.

It also includes configurable scenarios such as:

  • A shared illness-like physiological pattern across crew members.
  • A gradual 25-day stress-related physiological drift without fever.
  • Sensor signal dropouts, stale packets and high artifact ratios.
  • Mid-mission medical rebaselining.

3. Intelligence Without Losing Control

AeroMed combines statistical health analysis with intelligent assistance. While the system helps users understand complex health trends through natural-language explanations, all physiological alerts remain governed by predefined mathematical rules.

This allows intelligence to improve accessibility without compromising transparency or medical oversight.

4. Built for Deep-Space Communication Delays

The demonstration incorporates a 161-second communication delay to illustrate why onboard detection and autonomous decision support matter when communication with Earth isn't instantaneous.

5. Honest Device Integration

Simulated telemetry and real wearable integrations operate in separate modes. AeroMed does not claim that a device is connected without verified incoming sensor data.

Our aim was to combine meaningful health analytics with an interface that astronauts and medical officers can actually understand and use.

5. Things We Kept in Mind While Building AeroMed

Building something for spaceflight means thinking beyond whether the software simply works.

Safety Comes First

AeroMed is a non-diagnostic monitoring and decision-support platform. An urgent symptom flag allows an astronaut to raise a concern without waiting for automated trend detection. The software does not replace medical professionals or emergency procedures.

Trust Through Transparency

Every alert can be traced to specific readings and predefined rules. Proposed thresholds are clearly identified as requiring clinical validation. Wrist skin temperature is also distinguished from core body temperature.

Avoiding Alert Fatigue

Too many warnings can make people stop paying attention. That's why we introduced multi-signal agreement, persistence requirements and hysteresis to distinguish meaningful patterns from ordinary physiological fluctuations.

Privacy Matters

Different access roles are provided for Crew Members, Crew Medical Officers and Mission Researchers, with additional privacy considerations for sensitive behavioral health information.

Designed for Real Spaceflight Challenges

We considered irregular sleep schedules, missing readings, sensor artifacts, skewed HRV distributions and communication interruptions while designing the system.

Nothing Should Stop Working Just Because One Component Fails

AeroMed includes a 2D visualization fallback if 3D rendering is unavailable, polling if real-time streaming fails, and a deterministic Notes Assistant when external AI services or network connectivity are unavailable.

Being Honest About What We've Built

Our current demonstration uses a synthetic 45-day crew dataset informed by public PhysioNet data. The detection engine has automated tests and simulated scenarios, but its thresholds and clinical interpretations still require further validation before any operational medical use.

At its heart, AeroMed is built around one simple idea: Don't just monitor an astronaut's health. Understand how it changes over time.

Because on a mission where Earth is millions of kilometres away, noticing the little things early could matter a lot.
